q: Four regional credit unions want to split the cost of one cloud platform built to satisfy the same regulator-mandated audit controls. A single provider operates it, and only the four member institutions may use it. Which deployment model does this describe?
opts: Community cloud, shared by organizations with common compliance needs
Hybrid cloud, because the provider connects several separate tenants
Private cloud, because access is limited to a defined set of customers
Multi-cloud, because several organizations contribute to the platform
why: Community cloud is infrastructure shared by a small group of organizations with a common concern, here the same regulatory controls, and closed to the general public. Private cloud is dedicated to a single organization, so restricting access to a list of customers does not make it private. Hybrid means private and public environments connected together, which is not described. Multi-cloud means using more than one provider, but this platform has only one provider.

q: An application automatically adds server instances at 9 AM on weekdays and removes them at 6 PM, based on a fixed calendar schedule rather than real-time load. Which description is most accurate?
opts: Vertical scaling, because capacity changes at fixed times every day
Fault tolerance, since the system keeps running without any interruption during the schedule change
Elasticity, since it happens without manual intervention
Scheduled scaling, a form of scalability but not elasticity
why: This is automatic, but it is reacting to a calendar, not to real-time demand. Elasticity specifically means capacity that follows actual, current load. It also adds whole instances (horizontal), not a bigger existing one (vertical), and it has nothing to do with tolerating failures.

q: A single-instance licensed database is running out of memory. The vendor's license does not support clustering and the team has no time to re-architect, so they move the VM to a larger instance size. Which trade-off must they accept?
opts: Each additional instance must hold its own copy of the data, which can drift out of sync
It will likely need a restart, and it can only grow to the largest size offered
A load balancer becomes a single point of failure for all database connections
Capacity follows demand automatically, but only up to the autoscaling group's maximum
why: Resizing one instance is vertical scaling (scaling up). It usually needs a restart to apply and it hits a ceiling at the biggest instance size available. The other options describe consequences of horizontal scaling or autoscaling, which this team is not doing: replicas holding separate copies of data, a load balancer in front of the database, and elastic capacity bounded by a group maximum.

q: A database has an RPO of 15 minutes and an RTO of 4 hours. Transaction logs currently ship to the DR site hourly, and a rehearsed failover takes about 2 hours. Which single change brings the design into compliance?
opts: Automate failover so that it completes in under 15 minutes
Extend backup retention at the DR site from 7 to 30 days
Ship transaction logs to the DR site at least every 15 minutes
Add a second warm standby in a different region
why: The gap is data loss: hourly shipping can lose up to 60 minutes of transactions, which breaks a 15-minute RPO, so the shipping interval must shrink. The 2-hour failover already fits inside the 4-hour RTO, so speeding it up fixes nothing that is broken. Longer retention changes how far back you can restore, not how recent the newest copy is, and a second standby adds redundancy without changing the log-shipping interval.

q: A media company must retain several petabytes of finished video for seven years at the lowest cost. Files are written once, retrieved whole by a web application through HTTP API calls, and never edited in place. No application needs a mounted drive. Which storage type fits best?
opts: Object storage with lifecycle rules that move older files to cheaper tiers
Block storage volumes attached to a fleet of VMs, with snapshots
Instance-local ephemeral disks replicated across several hosts
File storage exposed to the application servers over SMB shares
why: Write-once, whole-file retrieval over HTTP at petabyte scale is the object storage use case, and lifecycle rules help control long-term cost. File storage adds a hierarchical, mountable filesystem that nothing here needs. Block storage is for low-latency random I/O such as a database disk. Ephemeral instance disks are lost when the instance stops, which is unacceptable for a seven-year retention requirement.

q: An application team wants one public address that sends requests for /api to a pool of API servers and requests for /images to a separate pool of media servers. Which load balancer approach can make that decision?
opts: A Layer 4 load balancer using the least-connections algorithm
A Layer 4 load balancer with source-IP affinity enabled
A Layer 7 (application-layer) load balancer that inspects HTTP request paths
DNS round robin returning each pool's addresses in rotation
why: Routing by URL path requires reading the HTTP request, which only a Layer 7 load balancer does. A Layer 4 balancer sees IP addresses and ports, so algorithms such as least connections or source-IP affinity only choose among servers in one pool and cannot tell /api from /images. DNS round robin hands out addresses in rotation before any request exists, so it has no visibility into the path at all.

q: Customers in Southeast Asia report slow page loads for static images served from a single origin in Europe. The origin's network link averages 15% utilization and its CPU is low. Which change most directly addresses the complaint?
opts: Upgrade the origin's network link to a higher bandwidth tier
Scale the origin vertically to a larger instance size
Add read replicas of the origin's database in the same region
Cache the static content at edge locations near those users with a CDN
why: Low link utilization and low CPU rule out a capacity problem, so the delay is distance: every request crosses the globe. A CDN caches content at edge locations close to users, cutting round-trip latency and offloading the origin. More bandwidth does not shorten the round trip, a bigger instance is not the bottleneck, and database replicas in the same region do nothing for static files served to distant users.

q: Which scenario describes a hybrid cloud deployment?
opts: A retailer runs its CRM at one public provider and its analytics at a second, with federated sign-on between them
A bank keeps customer records in an on-premises private cloud and bursts web workloads to a public provider over a dedicated link
A SaaS vendor replicates one public-cloud application between two regions of the same provider
Two subsidiaries each operate a separate private cloud in their own data centers, with no shared services
why: Hybrid cloud means private and public environments that are connected and coordinated, here an on-premises private cloud linked to a public provider so workloads can move or burst. Using two public providers, even with federated sign-on, is multi-cloud. Two unconnected private clouds are simply two private clouds, and replicating across regions of one provider is still a single public cloud deployment.

q: A cluster automatically promotes its standby node about 30 seconds after detecting a primary failure. Because the failover is automatic, the design qualifies as fault tolerant.
opts: True
False
why: Automatic failover is what makes a design highly available, but a 30-second promotion window is still an interruption that clients can see. Fault tolerance means the system keeps running through a failure with no interruption at all, which requires something like parallel processing across nodes and usually costs more. Automation and speed do not turn HA into fault tolerance.

q: Which two pairings of workload and storage type are appropriate? (Choose two.)
opts: A shared departmental folder mapped as a drive by desktop users, on object storage
Live data files of a transactional database, on block storage
A VM's boot disk, on file storage mounted over NFS
Seven years of nightly database dumps retrieved whole on demand, on object storage
Static website images, on block storage volumes attached to each web server
why: A transactional database needs low-latency random reads and writes, which is what block storage provides. Rarely-changed archives retrieved whole through an API are a natural fit for object storage's scale and low cost. A mapped drive for desktop users needs a hierarchical shared filesystem, which is file storage, not objects. A boot disk is block storage, and static images served to many users belong in object storage, not copied onto every web server's volume.

q: Which two actions are examples of horizontal scaling rather than vertical scaling? (Choose two.)
opts: Raising a container's CPU limit from 1 core to 4 cores
Raising a Kubernetes Deployment's replica count from 3 to 10
Enabling hot-add to grow a running VM's RAM from 8 GB to 32 GB
Replacing a VM's disk with a faster volume type
Adding two read replicas to a database to absorb read traffic
why: Horizontal scaling adds more instances working in parallel: more pod replicas and more database replicas both qualify. Giving one container more CPU, growing one VM's RAM, and swapping one VM's disk for a faster one all enlarge a single existing resource, which is vertical scaling even when no restart is needed.

q: An architect compares two payment API designs. Design 1: an active node with a standby promoted about 30 seconds after a health check fails. Design 2: three nodes process every request in parallel and a majority answer is accepted, so losing one node is invisible to clients. Which two statements are correct? (Choose two.)
opts: Design 1 is fault tolerant, because the standby is promoted automatically
Design 2 also provides disaster recovery, because it runs three copies of the service
Design 1 is highly available, but clients can still see a short interruption during promotion
Both designs have equivalent cost, because each runs several nodes
Design 2 is closer to fault tolerance, because one node failing causes no visible interruption
why: Design 1 minimizes downtime through redundancy, but the promotion window is a visible gap, so it is HA. Design 2 keeps answering through a node loss with no gap, which is the fault tolerance definition. Automatic promotion does not make Design 1 fault tolerant. Three nodes in one site do not protect against losing the whole site, so that is not disaster recovery, and parallel processing is generally more expensive than a mostly idle standby.

q: A startup uploads application code and a configuration file to a provider service. The provider supplies the runtime, patches the operating system, and adds instances as traffic grows. The startup cannot log in to the underlying servers or choose the OS version. Which service model is this?
opts: PaaS, because the provider manages the runtime and OS while the customer manages the code
IaaS with auto scaling, because instances are added as traffic grows
SaaS, because the provider operates everything above the hardware
A self-managed container platform, because instances are added automatically
why: Customer-supplied code on a provider-managed runtime and OS is PaaS. IaaS would leave OS patching and the server login to the customer, and auto scaling alone does not change that. SaaS delivers a finished application, but here the startup brings its own code. A self-managed container platform would mean the team operates the cluster, which contradicts the provider handling patching and scaling.

q: Two tenants' workloads share one physical host. A security review requires that a kernel vulnerability exploited in one tenant's workload cannot expose the other's. Cost is secondary. Which deployment best meets the requirement?
opts: Each workload in its own container, with separate CPU and memory limits
Both workloads in containers using separate namespaces and network segments
Each workload in its own VM, so each has a separate guest kernel behind the hypervisor
Both workloads on one VM, under separate non-privileged user accounts
why: A VM carries its own guest operating system, so a kernel exploit inside one VM is contained by the hypervisor boundary. Containers share the host's kernel, which is why they start quickly but are less isolated: namespaces, resource limits, and network segments all sit on top of the same kernel a vulnerability would target. User accounts on a single VM share one kernel as well.

q: A network team wants to push routing and segmentation policy to hundreds of physical and virtual switches from a central controller through an API, instead of logging in to each device. Which architecture provides this?
opts: A service mesh, which manages traffic between microservices using sidecar proxies
Software-defined networking, which separates the control plane from the data plane
A DMZ, which isolates public-facing servers between two firewalls
A content delivery network, which caches content at edge locations
why: SDN moves routing decisions into a central, programmable control plane while switches only forward packets, so policy is managed by software rather than device by device. A service mesh also uses central control, but it governs service-to-service traffic inside application clusters, not switch configuration. A CDN is about caching near users and a DMZ is a perimeter segmentation pattern; neither manages policy across switches.

q: Compared to a monolithic application, which two are genuine advantages of a microservices architecture? (Choose two.)
opts: Fewer network calls, because services no longer communicate across the network
Each service can scale independently based on its own load
Simpler end-to-end troubleshooting, because a request touches a single process
A failure in one service stays contained, so dependent services need no timeouts or circuit breakers
A team can deploy one service without redeploying the others
why: Independent scaling and independent deployment are the core benefits of splitting an application into services. The costs run the other way: services talk over the network, so there are more calls, tracing a request across many processes is harder, and a failing dependency can still cascade to its callers, which is exactly why timeouts and circuit breakers exist.

q: A regulated customer must guarantee that no other customer's workloads ever run on the physical hosts that run its VMs. Which offering meets this requirement?
opts: A private virtual network with customer-defined subnets and security rules
A separate account with its own billing and access policies
Dedicated hosts reserved exclusively for the customer's VMs
Customer-managed encryption keys on every VM disk and snapshot
why: Multitenancy means customers share physical infrastructure, isolated only logically. Guaranteeing no co-tenants requires single-tenant hardware such as dedicated hosts. Private virtual networks, separate accounts, and customer-managed keys are all useful logical isolation controls, but the VMs would still share physical hosts with other customers, which is exactly what the requirement forbids.

q: A team wants to scale a web tier horizontally to absorb traffic spikes, but each user's session data lives only in the local memory of whichever server first handled their login. Before adding more servers will actually spread that load, what has to change first?
opts: Switch the load balancing algorithm from round robin to least connections
Lengthen the load balancer's idle timeout so sessions outlive individual connections
Enable cross-zone balancing so requests spread evenly across availability zones
Put session data in a shared store (or use sticky sessions) so any server can handle any request
why: New servers cannot help a returning user whose session exists only in another server's memory. Either the session state moves to a shared external store so every server can read it, or sticky sessions pin each user to the server that holds their state. Changing the algorithm, lengthening idle timeouts, or balancing across zones changes how requests are distributed, but none of them makes a server able to find a session it never held.

q: A database cluster must guarantee that only one node ever accepts writes, so conflicting updates cannot occur. The budget allows the second node to sit idle until a failure. Which clustering model fits?
opts: Active-active, with a load balancer sending writes to both nodes
N+2 redundancy, with two spare nodes beyond what the load requires
Active-active, with each node owning a separate half of the data
Active-passive, with the standby promoted when the primary fails
why: In active-passive clustering one node serves and accepts writes while the standby waits, which is simple to keep consistent and wastes idle capacity by design. Active-active, either load-balancing writes or splitting the data between nodes, has more than one node accepting writes. N+2 describes how many spare units exist, not which node accepts writes.

q: A facility needs four generators to carry its full load and has five installed (N+1). If one generator is down for planned maintenance and another then fails unexpectedly, the facility is short of capacity.
opts: True
False
why: N+1 absorbs exactly one unit being unavailable. With one generator in maintenance and a second one failing, only three of the four required units remain. Surviving a planned outage plus a failure takes N+2, which is why higher N raises both resilience and ongoing cost.

q: Which two statements correctly describe Kubernetes objects? (Choose two.)
opts: A Deployment is the smallest deployable unit, wrapping one or more containers
A ReplicaSet replaces failed pods to keep the specified replica count
A pod manages ReplicaSets and performs rolling updates and rollbacks
A Service restarts crashed containers inside a pod
A Service gives clients a stable address even as pods are replaced
why: A ReplicaSet maintains a steady number of identical pods, and a Service provides a stable address that routes to whichever healthy pods currently exist. The other options swap the roles: the pod, not the Deployment, is the smallest deployable unit; the Deployment, not the pod, manages ReplicaSets and rolling updates; and restarting crashed containers is handled by the cluster's node agent and controllers, not by a Service.

q: After a breach, investigators confirm the attacker logged in with a valid stolen password and that the compromised role legitimately allowed the deletions. They cannot tell which records were deleted or when, because audit logging was disabled on the system. Which AAA function was missing?
opts: Authentication, which verifies the identity presenting credentials
Accounting, which records what each identity actually did
Authorization, which limits what a verified identity may do
Federation, which lets one identity provider vouch for users across systems
why: Accounting is the logging of what was actually done, and its absence is why the investigators cannot reconstruct the deletions. Authentication did its job in the narrow sense, since the credential was valid, and authorization did too, since the role permitted the actions. Federation is a way of sharing identities between systems and has no bearing on producing an audit trail.

q: A cloud team must let contractors reach only resources tagged with their own project, only during contract hours, and only from managed devices. New projects must not require creating new roles. Which access control model fits best?
opts: ABAC, evaluating user, resource, and context attributes at request time
MAC, with system-assigned classification labels on every resource
RBAC, with a distinct role created for each project
DAC, with each resource owner granting access individually
why: ABAC makes a decision per request from attributes such as the contractor's project, the resource's tag, the time, and device posture, so a new project needs only a new tag value, not a new role. RBAC would need a role per project and cannot express time or device conditions natively. MAC relies on centrally assigned classification labels, and DAC leaves grants to individual owners, which does not scale or enforce these contextual rules.

q: A database volume is fully encrypted on disk, yet an attacker intercepted query results as they traveled from the database server to a reporting application over an internal network. Which control would most directly have prevented the interception?
opts: Rotating the disk-encryption key more frequently
Requiring MFA for database administrator logins
Enabling transparent encryption on the reporting application's local cache
Enforcing TLS between the reporting application and the database
why: The data was intercepted while moving across the network, so the missing control is encryption in transit, such as TLS on the database connection. Disk encryption was already in place and protects only stored data, so rotating its key does nothing for traffic on the wire. MFA governs who can log in, and encrypting the application's cache protects another at-rest copy, not the connection.

q: A team wants to detect network attacks but guarantee that the detection tool can never interrupt production traffic, even on a false positive. Which deployment meets that requirement?
opts: An inline IPS configured to drop packets that match attack signatures
A passive IDS fed a copy of traffic from a network tap or mirror port
A WAF in blocking mode placed in front of the web servers
An inline IPS configured to fail closed if its inspection engine stops
why: A passive IDS only sees a copy of the traffic and raises alerts, so a false positive produces a noisy alert rather than an outage. An inline IPS sits in the traffic path and acts on matches, so a false positive drops legitimate packets, and failing closed makes an engine fault block traffic too. A WAF in blocking mode is likewise inline and can reject legitimate requests.

q: An engineer adds an inbound allow rule for TCP 443 to a subnet-level filter. The web servers are healthy and their instance-level firewalls allow the traffic, yet clients still time out. The subnet filter evaluates each packet independently. What is most likely missing?
opts: An IPS policy that explicitly trusts the clients' source addresses
A connection-tracking table large enough to hold all active sessions
An outbound rule on the subnet filter permitting the servers' reply traffic
A signature update so the filter recognizes HTTPS traffic
why: A filter that evaluates every packet independently is stateless, so it does not recognize replies as belonging to an allowed connection; the response leaving the subnet needs its own outbound rule. A stateless filter keeps no connection table, so table size is irrelevant, and it uses simple rules rather than signatures or IPS trust policies.

q: A payment processor wants application servers to hold no recoverable form of stored card numbers, yet customer service must still be able to retrieve the original number for a refund through a controlled lookup. Which technique fits?
opts: Tokenization, with the real numbers held in a separate secured vault
Salted hashing of each card number before it is stored
Masking all but the last four digits when the number is stored
Symmetric encryption, with the key stored on the application server
why: Tokenization stores a meaningless substitute on the application side and keeps the real number only in a separate vault, so the original can be retrieved through a controlled lookup but cannot be computed from the token. Encryption with a locally stored key leaves a recoverable form on the same server. Hashing is one-way, so the number could never be retrieved for a refund, and masking discards the digits it hides.

q: After an attacker used a stolen VPN credential to join the internal network, an organization adopts Zero Trust. Which outcome would Zero Trust most directly have prevented?
opts: The credential being phished from the user in the first place
The VPN requiring authentication at connect time
Reaching sensitive systems on the strength of network access alone
Any need to log or audit the attacker's later activity
why: Zero Trust never grants trust based on network location, so being inside the network is not enough: each request to a sensitive system is verified on its own. It does not stop credential theft itself, it adds verification rather than removing it, and it increases rather than eliminates the need for logging and auditing.

q: A security team replaces an out-of-band IDS with an inline IPS using the same signature set. Shortly afterward, a partner's legitimate API calls begin failing. Which statement best explains why this could happen only after the change?
opts: The IPS cannot inspect encrypted traffic, so partner sessions are reset
An IPS only alerts, so the partner's underlying problem went unnoticed
Inline placement lets a false-positive signature match drop legitimate packets
The same signature set behaves differently on an IPS than on an IDS
why: An IDS only alerts, so a false-positive signature was harmless. An IPS sits inline and acts on matches, so the same false positive now drops real traffic, which is the main operational risk of prevention. The signature logic is identical in both tools, an IPS blocks rather than only alerts, and inability to inspect encrypted traffic would not start resetting sessions.

q: Because a database volume is encrypted at rest, requiring TLS for client connections adds no meaningful protection.
opts: True
False
why: At-rest encryption protects data on disk, for example when a volume or snapshot is copied. Query results travelling to a client cross the network in a different state, and only encryption in transit such as TLS protects them there. Neither control substitutes for the other.

q: Which two statements correctly contrast security groups and network ACLs (NACLs)? (Choose two.)
opts: A NACL applies at the instance interface, while a security group applies at the subnet boundary
A security group's allow rule for inbound traffic automatically permits the matching reply
A security group is stateless, so return traffic needs its own explicit rule
A NACL needs separate inbound and outbound rules for the two directions of a connection
Both evaluate packets using connection state
why: A security group is stateful, so approving a request automatically approves its response. A NACL is stateless and judges each direction independently, so both directions need rules. The scope statement is swapped: security groups apply at the instance or interface level and NACLs at the subnet level. Calling a security group stateless, or saying both use connection state, is also wrong.

q: If an attacker steals a database containing only tokens that replaced card numbers, they obtain no usable card data unless they also compromise the separate token vault.
opts: True
False
why: A token has no mathematical relationship to the original value, so it cannot be reversed by computation, even with unlimited computing power. The original is recoverable only by looking the token up in the vault, which is why the vault, not the tokenized database, becomes the asset that must be protected.

q: Which two measures best implement Zero Trust for administrators who reach a production database from home? (Choose two.)
opts: Allowing all traffic from the VPN address range once login succeeds
Authorizing each request using identity and device posture, not network location
Trusting any device that connects from the corporate IP range
Micro-segmentation with default-deny rules between workloads
Strengthening the perimeter firewall's inbound rules as the primary control
why: Zero Trust verifies every request on identity, device posture, and context, and limits lateral movement by denying traffic between workloads unless it is explicitly allowed. Trusting a VPN range or corporate IP range, or relying chiefly on the perimeter, are all location-based trust, which is the assumption Zero Trust removes.

q: A backup tape containing a database dump is lost in transit. Which two measures would have protected the data? (Choose two.)
opts: Requiring TLS on the network path used by the backup job
Encrypting the backup files before they are written to tape
Segmenting the backup network from the production network
Storing the decryption keys separately from the tape media
Hashing each backup file and recording the digest
why: A lost tape is data at rest, so the protections are encryption of the stored files and keeping the keys somewhere other than the tape. TLS protects data moving across a network, segmentation limits network exposure, and a hash proves integrity but does nothing to keep the contents unreadable.

q: A company wants a genuine second authentication factor added to its password-only login. Which change achieves that?
opts: Adding a security question about the user's first pet
Requiring a second, different password after the first is accepted
Raising the minimum passphrase length to 20 characters
Requiring a code from an authenticator app on the user's enrolled phone
why: An app-generated one-time code proves possession of the enrolled phone, a "something you have" factor that differs in category from a password. A security question, a second password, and a longer passphrase are all still "something you know," so the login remains single-factor no matter how many knowledge checks are stacked.

q: A network firewall allows TCP 443 to a public web application. Attackers send valid HTTPS requests containing SQL injection payloads, and the requests pass straight through. Which added control inspects request content after TLS is terminated?
opts: A web application firewall (WAF) in front of the application
A network IDS monitoring the subnet without decrypting traffic
A CDN configured to cache more of the static content
A stateful firewall with stricter source-address rules
why: The requests are legitimate-looking HTTPS to an allowed port, so only a control that reads the HTTP payload can catch SQL injection; a WAF does that where TLS is already terminated. Tightening a network firewall still judges by address and port, a network IDS that cannot decrypt sees only ciphertext, and a CDN's caching does not inspect request content.

q: Compliance requires that encryption keys be generated and used inside tamper-resistant hardware so raw key material never appears in operating system or application memory. Which solution meets this?
opts: An encrypted key file protected by operating system file permissions
A secrets manager that stores keys as encrypted database records
A key derived from a long passphrase each time the application starts
A hardware security module (HSM) that performs cryptographic operations internally
why: An HSM generates, stores, and uses keys inside dedicated tamper-resistant hardware, so applications ask it to perform operations and never receive the raw key. The other approaches all load key material into software memory at some point: a key file, a secrets store's decrypted record, or a passphrase-derived key.

q: A developer needs to restart VMs in one project for the next two weeks. Which grant best follows least privilege?
opts: The built-in contributor role on the project, removed manually afterward
A custom role limited to VM restart on that project, expiring after two weeks
Read-only access across the whole subscription plus a shared admin password
The owner role on the project, with MFA required for sign-in
why: Least privilege means the minimum permissions, scope, and duration the task needs: VM restart only, one project only, and an automatic expiry. The contributor and owner roles grant far more than restarting VMs, and relying on manual removal or MFA does not reduce what the role can do. A shared admin password is both over-broad and unaccountable.

q: During a TLS handshake, the client and server use a slow asymmetric exchange to agree on a secret, then switch algorithms for the bulk of the session. Which statement best explains the switch?
opts: Symmetric encryption is much faster for large data, and both sides now share the same key
Hashing replaces encryption once the certificate has been validated
Asymmetric keys expire after the handshake, so they cannot protect later traffic
Symmetric encryption is stronger per bit, so it is reserved for session data
why: Asymmetric operations are computationally expensive, so TLS uses them only to authenticate and establish a shared secret, then encrypts the bulk data symmetrically, which is far faster. Asymmetric keys do not expire at the end of the handshake, a hash is a one-way digest rather than a way to encrypt data, and symmetric algorithms are chosen for speed, not because they are stronger per bit.

q: One tool passively monitors network traffic and raises an alert when it recognizes a known attack signature, without blocking anything. A second platform ingests those alerts alongside logs from many other systems and correlates them into a single case for an analyst to review. Which tools are these, in order?
opts: An IPS, then a SIEM
An IDS, then a SOAR platform
A SIEM, then an IDS
An IDS, then a SIEM
why: A tool that only alerts is an IDS, and one that correlates alerts and logs for an analyst to review is a SIEM. An IPS would sit inline and block matching traffic. A SOAR platform goes further by triggering automated response actions rather than presenting a case for a person, and a SIEM cannot precede the IDS because it needs alerts and logs to ingest first.

q: A web server must accept connections from the internet, and its compromise must not give an attacker a direct path to the internal database network. Which design best meets both goals?
opts: Place it on the internal LAN, with the perimeter firewall forwarding port 443 to it
Place it in a DMZ subnet, with only the required DMZ-to-database flow allowed inward
Place it on the database VLAN, protected by a host-based firewall
Keep it on the internal LAN and add mutual TLS between it and the database
why: A DMZ puts internet-facing servers in their own segment between firewalls, so only the specific flows they need can reach internal systems and a compromise stays contained. Placing the server on the LAN or on the database VLAN puts it directly beside the assets to protect, and mutual TLS authenticates connections but does not stop an attacker already on the LAN from moving laterally.

q: A CI service account's key leaks from a public repository. The key only had read access to one storage bucket, so the attacker could read that bucket and nothing else. Which principle limited the damage?
opts: Least privilege, because the key was scoped to only what its job required
Defense in depth, because several independent control layers stood in the way
Credential rotation, because the key was replaced on a regular schedule
Zero Trust, because every request was re-verified regardless of source
why: The limit on what the leaked key could reach comes from scoping it to read-only access on one bucket, which is least privilege. Zero Trust re-verification would still pass a valid key, defense in depth describes stacked layers rather than the size of one grant, and rotation limits how long a key stays valid, not how much it can access while it is valid.

q: A security group that allows inbound TCP 443 and has no outbound allow rules at all still lets the server reply to those requests.
opts: True
False
why: Security groups are stateful: once a request is allowed in, its response is automatically allowed back out without a matching outbound rule. This is the contrast with a stateless network ACL, where the reply direction needs an explicit rule of its own.

q: A SIEM correlates alerts for analysts. The security team now wants a high-confidence alert to disable the compromised account automatically, before any analyst reviews it. Which capability must be added?
opts: Lower alert thresholds in the SIEM's correlation rules
SOAR playbooks that trigger response actions from SIEM detections
An inline IPS at the network edge to drop the attacker's packets
A WAF in front of the identity provider's login page
why: SOAR adds automated response on top of detection, so a playbook can disable an account the moment a qualifying SIEM alert fires. Lower thresholds only produce more alerts for humans to handle. An IPS blocks packets but does not manage accounts, and a WAF inspects web requests at one login page rather than responding to a detection by disabling an identity.

q: A developer accidentally commits a live API key to a public repository. Which two actions most directly reduce the risk? (Choose two.)
opts: Delete the file in a new commit so it no longer appears in the repository
Revoke the exposed key and issue a replacement
Require MFA on the developer's account
Review access logs for any use of the key since the commit
Enable encryption at rest on the storage the key can reach
why: The key must be assumed compromised, so revoking and rotating it ends its usefulness, and checking logs shows whether it was already used. Deleting the file in a new commit leaves the key in the repository history and in anyone's clone. MFA on the developer's account does not affect a bearer key, and at-rest encryption does not stop an authorized key from reading data.

q: A release changes an API contract, so the old and new versions should not serve users side by side. The business wants a rollback measured in seconds and will fund a temporary duplicate of production. Which deployment strategy fits?
opts: Canary deployment, shifting a small percentage of traffic to the new version first
Rolling deployment, updating a few instances at a time behind the load balancer
In-place deployment, updating every server directly during a maintenance window
Blue-green deployment, switching all traffic to a fully verified duplicate environment
why: Blue-green keeps two identical environments, verifies the idle one, and then switches all traffic at once, so users see one version or the other, and rollback is just switching back. Canary and rolling deployments deliberately run both versions together while the rollout progresses, which the API change forbids. An in-place update has neither a duplicate to fall back on nor a seconds-long rollback.

q: A company runs a full backup every Sunday and a differential backup every other day of the week. If a failure happens on Thursday, which backups are needed to fully restore the data, and in what order?
opts: Sunday's full backup, then every differential from Monday through Wednesday, in sequence
Sunday's full backup, then Thursday's differential backup
Only Wednesday's differential backup
Sunday's full backup, then Wednesday's differential backup
why: A differential backup captures everything changed since the last FULL backup, so the most recent differential (Wednesday's) already contains all of Monday through Wednesday's changes on its own — only the full plus that single latest differential are needed. Needing to replay every differential in sequence is the restore pattern for incremental backups, not differential.

q: Two years ago a physical server was converted to a VM on the company's on-premises hypervisor. The team now exports that VM image and imports it unchanged into a provider's public cloud compute service. Which migration type is this move?
opts: P2C, because the workload originally ran on physical hardware
V2C, because the source was already virtualized on-premises
V2V, because the VM is moving to a different hypervisor
P2V, because the server is being converted into a virtual machine
why: The migration type is set by the state of the source right now: a workload that is already a VM on-premises and is moving into the cloud is V2C. Its physical past and the earlier P2V conversion are history. V2V would keep the VM on a hypervisor environment rather than moving it into the provider's cloud service, and P2C requires the source to still be physical.

q: A storage administrator allocates 500 GB volumes to twenty different servers on a storage array that only physically has 3 TB of actual capacity, on the assumption that most volumes won't use their full allocation at once. Which approach is this, and what is its main risk?
opts: Thin provisioning — if many volumes fill at once, the array can run out of physical space while each volume still shows free space
Thin provisioning — one volume filling up corrupts the data on every other volume on the array
Thin provisioning — the array reserves the full 500 GB per volume up front, so unused space is stranded
Thick provisioning — the array wastes capacity because each volume's full size is reserved immediately
why: Allocating more logical capacity than physically exists is thin provisioning, and its central risk is aggregate demand: if enough volumes actually fill, the physical storage runs out even though each volume still reports free space. Reserving the full size up front is thick provisioning, which this scenario explicitly is not doing, and one volume filling does not corrupt its neighbors.

q: A team must create identical networks, subnets, and VMs in dev, test, and production from version-controlled definitions, and detect when someone changes a resource by hand in the console. Which approach fits best?
opts: A configuration management tool that installs packages on servers that already exist
A golden VM image cloned manually into each environment
A CI pipeline that runs unit tests against the application on each commit
Declarative IaC templates in version control, applied by a provisioning tool
why: Declarative infrastructure-as-code templates describe the networks, subnets, and VMs themselves, produce the same result in every environment, and let the provisioning tool compare the declared state to what actually exists to reveal manual changes. Configuration management shapes software and settings on machines that already exist rather than creating the network layer, CI testing validates application code, and a hand-cloned image creates neither networks nor drift detection.

q: After every change passes automated tests, the pipeline packages it and keeps it in a release-ready state. A product owner then presses a button to release it to production whenever the business chooses. Which practice is this?
opts: Continuous deployment, because passing changes are packaged automatically
Continuous delivery, because release is a manual decision
A canary release, because production gets a gradual rollout
Continuous integration, because changes are merged and tested frequently
why: Keeping every passing change releasable while a human decides when to release is continuous delivery. Continuous deployment removes that human gate so every passing change ships automatically. Continuous integration covers only the frequent merge-and-test step, and a canary release is a rollout technique that nothing in the scenario describes.

q: A company takes a full backup on Sunday and incremental backups Monday through Wednesday. The server fails Thursday morning, and Tuesday's incremental file turns out to be corrupt. What is the most recent state the company can restore using only these backups?
opts: Monday's state, because the chain of incrementals breaks at the corrupt Tuesday file
Wednesday's state, because Wednesday's incremental contains everything since Sunday
Sunday's state only, because any corrupt incremental invalidates the whole set
Wednesday's state, because incrementals are independent and can be applied in any order
why: An incremental backup holds only what changed since the previous backup, so a restore needs the full backup plus every incremental in sequence. The chain works through Monday, then breaks at the corrupt Tuesday file, so Wednesday's changes cannot be applied. Wednesday would hold everything only if it were a differential, and applying incrementals out of order or independently does not work.

q: A team wants a small percentage of live traffic to reach the new version first, raising that percentage only while error rates stay low. They do not want to maintain a full duplicate environment. Which strategy fits?
opts: Blue-green deployment, switching all traffic after verifying the idle environment
Rolling deployment, replacing instances a batch at a time until all are updated
Canary release, shifting a small share of traffic and raising it as metrics hold
In-place deployment, upgrading each server directly in one window
why: A canary release exposes the new version to a controlled slice of traffic and widens it as confidence grows, limiting the blast radius without a second full environment. Blue-green needs a full duplicate and switches everyone at once. A rolling deployment proceeds by batches of instances until all are updated, not by a traffic percentage gated on error rates, and an in-place upgrade exposes everyone with no gradual control.

q: Which two outcomes does defining an environment in version-controlled IaC most directly enable? (Choose two.)
opts: Removing the need to back up the data stored in the environment
Reviewing infrastructure changes through the same pull-request process as application code
Scaling the environment up and down automatically as load changes
Rebuilding an identical environment in another region from the same definition
Guaranteeing no drift even when manual console changes remain permitted
why: Because the infrastructure is described in files, changes can be reviewed, versioned, and audited like source code, and the same definition can be deployed again elsewhere to get the same result. IaC does not replace data backups, since it recreates infrastructure, not the data inside it. It does not by itself add autoscaling behavior, and drift can still happen if people are allowed to change resources by hand.

q: Which two statements correctly compare rolling and blue-green deployments? (Choose two.)
opts: Rolling keeps two identical environments and switches all traffic at once
Rolling needs no duplicate environment, but old and new versions serve users together mid-rollout
Blue-green exposes the new version to a small share of users first
Blue-green rolls back quickly because the old environment keeps running until retired
Blue-green needs no extra capacity, since traffic is simply redirected
why: A rolling deployment updates instances a few at a time inside the existing environment, so no duplicate is needed, but during the rollout both versions are live. Blue-green's fast rollback comes from the previous environment still running. The other statements are mixed up: keeping two environments and switching all traffic at once describes blue-green, gradual exposure to a small share of users is canary, and blue-green does require capacity for the second environment.

q: New checkout code must be running in production days before launch, then be switched on or off instantly for chosen customer segments, without redeploying or shifting traffic between environments. Which technique fits?
opts: Blue-green deployment, with the cutover scheduled for launch time
Feature flags, which gate the new code path at runtime for chosen segments
Rolling deployment, updating a few instances at a time
Canary release, increasing the share of traffic sent to the new version
why: Feature flags decouple deployment (getting code into production) from release (exposing it), so the code can sit dormant and be toggled per segment with no new deployment. Blue-green switches whole environments, canary controls a percentage of traffic by shifting it to a new version, and a rolling deployment changes which version instances run; each of those is itself a deployment action rather than a runtime switch.

q: A disaster recovery tabletop exercise, in which stakeholders walk through the plan step by step, proves that failover will complete within the stated RTO.
opts: True
False
why: A tabletop exercise is a discussion that exposes gaps in the plan, roles, and communication without moving any services. Because nothing is actually failed over, it cannot show how long the real recovery takes; only a live or full-interruption test measures that against the RTO.

q: A team's policy is that nobody logs in to change a running server. Every patch is baked into a new image that replaces the old instance. Which principle is this?
opts: Configuration management, because desired state is re-applied to running servers hourly
Immutable infrastructure, because running instances are replaced rather than modified
Rolling deployment, because instances are patched in place a few at a time
Blue-green deployment, because two environments exist side by side
why: Immutable infrastructure means an instance is never modified after it is provisioned; a change means building and deploying a replacement. Configuration management and in-place rolling patches both modify running servers, which is exactly what this policy prohibits. Blue-green describes cutting traffic over between two environments, not a rule against changing running instances, though the two can be combined.

q: A blue-green rollback is instant only while the old environment is still running; once it has been decommissioned, rolling back means redeploying it.
opts: True
False
why: Blue-green's instant rollback comes from keeping the previous environment alive after cutover and simply switching traffic back. That duplicate costs money, so teams retire it after a confidence period, and after that a rollback is an ordinary redeployment of the old version.

q: A company moves an on-premises application to cloud VMs but replaces its self-managed MySQL server with the provider's managed MySQL service. The application code is unchanged. Which migration strategy is this?
opts: Rehost, which moves everything exactly as it is, with no component swapped
Refactor, which redesigns the application around cloud-native services
Repurchase, which replaces the application with a different SaaS product
Replatform, which makes light optimizations without changing the architecture
why: Swapping one component for a managed equivalent while leaving the application's design and code alone is replatforming. Rehost would move the database server unchanged, refactor would redesign the application itself, and repurchase would drop the application for a different product altogether.

q: After a hotfix to the discount calculation, QA reruns the existing suites for checkout, search, and login, which all passed last release, to confirm nothing else broke. Which type of testing is this?
opts: Functional testing of the new discount rule against its specification
Regression testing, confirming previously working features still work
Performance testing of checkout under expected peak load
Usability testing with a group of real shoppers
why: Re-running previously passing tests after a change to confirm that nothing else broke is regression testing. Functional testing checks that the changed feature meets its specification, which is a different question. Performance testing measures behavior under load and usability testing evaluates how easily people can use the result.

q: A staging environment with a much smaller database and fewer nodes than production is still adequate for validating how a release will behave under production load.
opts: True
False
why: Staging is meant to mirror production as closely as practical. A scaled-down copy can confirm functionality, but problems that depend on data volume, concurrency, or cluster size, such as slow queries on large tables or coordination issues between many nodes, will not show up until production.

q: A team's staging environment has two web nodes and a 5 GB sample database, while production has twenty nodes and a 4 TB database. Which two problems is staging most likely to miss before release? (Choose two.)
opts: A syntax error in the application's configuration file
A query that is fast on 5 GB but takes minutes on 4 TB
A feature that returns the wrong value for a given input
A race condition that only appears when many nodes coordinate
A missing database column required by the new release
why: Staging's value comes from resembling production, and here it differs in data volume and cluster size. Query performance at large scale and coordination issues among many nodes depend on exactly those differences, so they can slip through. A configuration syntax error, wrong output for an input, and a missing column would all appear in a small environment just as clearly.

q: During a rolling deployment of a new application version, error rates spike on the updated instances. Which preparation, made before the rollout, would let the team revert cleanly instead of improvising?
opts: A longer maintenance window so the rollout can proceed more slowly
A fresh full backup of the application database taken just before the rollout
Stricter health checks that remove failing instances from rotation
A tested rollback procedure, with the prior version's artifacts retained for redeploy
why: A rolling deployment has no duplicate environment to switch back to, so a tested, prepared rollback plan with the previous version still available is what makes reverting clean. Stricter health checks only take bad instances out of service, shrinking capacity without restoring the old version. A database backup protects data rather than the application version, and a longer window just slows the same rollout.

q: After failing over to a DR site and running there for several days, returning to the primary site requires reconciling the changes made at the DR site first, or data can be lost.
opts: True
False
why: Failback is a separate step from failover with its own risk. Transactions written at the DR site while it served production exist nowhere else, so they must be synchronized to the restored primary before switching back, or they will be lost or conflict. DR tests that rehearse only failover often miss this.

q: Which of the following is an example of orchestration rather than automation of a single task?
opts: A watchdog that automatically restarts a service when it crashes
A scheduled script that rotates and archives log files every night
A workflow that provisions a VM, configures it, and adds it to a load balancer in order
A runbook document that lists the manual steps for building a new server
why: Orchestration coordinates several automated tasks into one end-to-end workflow, here provisioning, configuring, and registering in order. The watchdog and the log-rotation script are each a single automated task. A runbook documents steps for a person or tool to follow but does not itself execute or sequence anything.

q: Finance wants every department to see its monthly cloud cost this quarter as an awareness exercise. Departmental budgets will not be debited until allocation rules are agreed. Which approach fits?
opts: Showback, reporting each department's usage and cost without moving funds
Budget caps that block provisioning once a department's limit is reached
Reserved-instance purchasing to lower the per-hour rate for all departments
Chargeback, debiting each department's budget for its usage
why: Showback reports cost for visibility and accountability without any transfer of money, which matches the quarter's goal. Chargeback actually debits budgets, which the scenario rules out for now. Budget caps are an enforcement control and reserved instances are a purchasing discount; neither gives departments a view of what they spent.

q: An alert for CPU above 90% pages the team every night at 2 AM, when a scheduled batch job normally pushes CPU to about 95%. Which step was skipped before this threshold was set?
opts: Writing a runbook for the alert's first-response steps
Negotiating an SLA for the batch job's completion time
Observing a baseline of normal behavior, including the nightly batch
Recording the server as a configuration item in the CMDB
why: A baseline captures what normal looks like over time, including predictable patterns such as a nightly batch. A threshold set without one tends to misfire on ordinary behavior, exactly as here. A runbook helps responders act but does not prevent a bad threshold, an SLA sets service commitments, and a CMDB entry records an asset and its relationships, not its normal utilization.

q: A provider's SLA promises 99.9% uptime per month, measured over a 30-day month. Two outages occurred this month, lasting 20 minutes and 30 minutes. Was the commitment met?
opts: Yes, because each individual outage was shorter than the roughly 43 minutes allowed
No, because 99.9% permits no more than about 4 minutes of downtime per month
Yes, because 99.9% permits about 8.75 hours of downtime in a month
No, because 50 minutes of downtime exceeds the roughly 43 minutes that 99.9% allows
why: A 30-day month has 43,200 minutes, and 0.1% of that is about 43 minutes. Downtime is cumulative, so 20 plus 30 minutes is 50 minutes and the target was missed. Judging each outage separately ignores the total, about 4 minutes per month is closer to 99.99%, and 8.75 hours is the allowance per year, not per month.

q: A team has scripted each step of building a new server separately: create the VM, install the software, join the load balancer. A person still runs each script by hand in the right order. What is missing before this counts as orchestration?
opts: A runbook that documents the exact order in which to run each script
A baseline of how long each script normally takes to finish
A CMDB entry recording each script as a configuration item
A workflow engine that sequences the scripts and passes results between them
why: The individual steps are already automated; what is missing is the coordination layer that runs them in order, passes outputs from one to the next, and handles failures. A runbook documents the sequence for a person, which is exactly the manual coordination described. A baseline and a CMDB entry describe normal behavior and assets, not execution.

q: Showback requires accurate, consistent resource tagging just as chargeback does, even though no money moves between departments.
opts: True
False
why: Both models depend on attributing each resource's cost to the right owner, and tags are what make that attribution automatic. If the numbers shown to departments are wrong, showback loses credibility long before any budget is debited, so the tagging discipline matters equally.

q: Which two statements about SLAs are correct? (Choose two.)
opts: A 99.99% target allows more downtime than a 99.9% target
A 99.9% target over a 30-day month allows about 43 minutes of total downtime
A provider meeting its uptime SLA guarantees the customer's own RTO is met
The usual remedy for a missed target is a service credit, not repayment of the customer's lost revenue
An SLA's uptime figure normally includes outages caused by the customer's own misconfiguration
why: 99.9% of a 30-day month leaves about 43 minutes, and SLA remedies are typically service credits rather than compensation for the customer's business losses. More nines means less allowed downtime, so 99.99% is stricter. An SLA covers the provider's service, not the customer's own recovery objectives, and it normally excludes outages the customer causes.

q: Which two tasks are examples of orchestration rather than single-task automation? (Choose two.)
opts: A watchdog that automatically restarts a service when it crashes
A pipeline that provisions an environment, deploys, tests, and tears it down
A policy that stops all development VMs every night at 7 PM
A scheduled script that rotates and archives log files every night
A workflow that rolls back a failed release, notifies the team, and opens a ticket
why: Orchestration chains multiple automated steps into one workflow with sequencing and hand-offs: provision, deploy, test, and tear down, or roll back, notify, and ticket. The watchdog restart, the nightly stop policy, and the log rotation script are each a single well-defined task that runs on its own.

q: A team has requested a patch change, tested it in staging, and received approval for an upcoming maintenance window. Which element of a formal change process should still be ready BEFORE the change is implemented?
opts: An updated CMDB record showing the new patch level
A documented rollback plan for reverting the change if it fails
A blameless review of how the patch rollout went
A showback report for the cost of the maintenance window
why: A formal change includes a rollback plan prepared before the change is made, so the team can revert quickly if the patch misbehaves. The CMDB should be updated after the change is completed so that it reflects the real state, and a review of how the rollout went can only happen afterward. A cost report has no role in whether the change can be safely made.

q: A team reviews a year of storage utilization, sees steady growth of about 10% per quarter, and orders more capacity before the array fills. Which practice does this describe?
opts: Right-sizing, adjusting allocations to match observed usage
Elasticity, adding resources automatically as demand rises
Capacity planning, forecasting future needs from historical trends
Root cause analysis, investigating why consumption changed
why: Using historical trends to forecast demand and provision ahead of it is capacity planning. Right-sizing adjusts existing allocations to match actual use, typically downward, elasticity reacts automatically to current demand rather than to a forecast, and root cause analysis investigates incidents after the fact.

q: A runbook is only useful when a person follows it; automation tooling cannot execute one.
opts: True
False
why: A runbook is a documented, repeatable procedure, and its value is that it produces the same result no matter who or what carries it out. Well-written runbooks are commonly turned into scripts or workflows that automation and orchestration tools trigger without a person doing each step.

q: A critical vulnerability is being actively exploited and cannot wait for the next change advisory meeting. Which two actions are consistent with a formal change process? (Choose two.)
opts: Skip the rollback plan, since the emergency leaves no time to prepare one
Obtain expedited approval from a designated emergency approver
Bypass all approval, since emergencies are exempt from change control
Defer logging the change until the next audit is scheduled
Record the change in the CMDB and hold a review afterward
why: Emergency changes still go through a compressed version of the process: a designated approver signs off quickly, and the change is documented and reviewed afterward so the record stays accurate. Skipping the rollback plan, bypassing approval entirely, or postponing documentation is how emergency fixes become the next outage.

q: Monitoring shows several steady, 24x7 production VMs average 15% CPU and memory use. The team wants to cut cost without hurting performance. Which action should come first?
opts: Buy three-year reserved instances at the current size to lock in the discount
Move the VMs to spot instances to get the deepest discount
Right-size to smaller instance types first, then commit to the new size
Add autoscaling so extra instances are created when load rises
why: Right-sizing removes the waste first, and a reservation made afterward then discounts the right size. Reserving the current size would lock in a three-year commitment on capacity that is mostly idle. Spot instances can be reclaimed with little notice, which steady production workloads cannot tolerate, and autoscaling adds capacity when load rises, which does nothing about overprovisioned VMs.

q: A nightly backup job has reported "completed successfully" for two years. That is enough evidence the data can be restored, so scheduled test restores add little value.
opts: True
False
why: A successful job status only shows the backup process ran without error. The file could still be corrupt, incomplete, or missing something needed for recovery, and you only discover that by restoring. Periodic test restores are what prove recoverability and also show how long a restore really takes.

q: A CPU alert set from a solid baseline still pages the on-call team dozens of times a day for spikes that self-resolve within seconds. Which adjustment most directly addresses this without hiding a real, sustained problem?
opts: Raise the threshold so far that only near-total CPU saturation fires it
Shorten the polling interval so each spike is detected sooner
Require the breach to persist for a set period before the alert fires
Route the alert to a shared inbox instead of the pager
why: A sustained-duration condition ignores brief self-clearing spikes while still firing if the threshold stays breached. Raising the threshold to near saturation would also miss serious but sub-saturation problems, polling more often only catches more spikes, and moving the alert to an inbox hides the noise rather than fixing the detection logic.

q: Before decommissioning a legacy database server, engineers need to know which applications and teams depend on it. Which resource is designed to answer that?
opts: The CMDB, which records configuration items and the relationships between them
A runbook describing how to restore the server from backup
A performance baseline showing the server's normal utilization
Resource tags recording the server's department and environment
why: A CMDB tracks IT assets and the relationships between them, so it can answer what depends on this server and who owns those services. Tags record attributes such as department but not dependency relationships, a baseline describes normal resource use, and a runbook explains how to carry out a procedure.

q: A team runs a steady 24x7 production database for the next three years and a rendering job that checkpoints its progress and can restart if interrupted. Which purchasing pairing minimizes cost without adding risk?
opts: Spot instances for the database, reserved instances for the rendering job
On-demand instances for both, to avoid any long-term commitment
Reserved instances for the database, spot instances for the rendering job
Reserved instances for both, to get the largest commitment discount
why: A steady, predictable workload is what reserved capacity discounts reward, and an interruptible, restartable job is what spot capacity's deep discount suits. Putting the database on spot risks losing it mid-transaction when capacity is reclaimed. On-demand for both pays the highest rate, and reserving a job that may run only occasionally commits money to capacity that sits idle.

q: A service rarely fails, but each failure takes about five hours to resolve because engineers rebuild it by hand. Which metric is the weak point, and which investment improves it most directly?
opts: MTTR is the weak point; scripted recovery and runbooks would shorten each repair
MTBF is the weak point, because failures are expensive to repair
MTBF is the weak point; more frequent health checks would lengthen the time between failures
RPO is the weak point; more frequent backups would shorten each repair
why: Rare failures mean MTBF, the average time between failures, is already good. Five-hour repairs mean MTTR is high, and the fix is faster recovery through runbooks and scripted rebuilds. Health checks detect failures rather than prevent them, MTBF measures frequency and not repair cost, and RPO concerns acceptable data loss, which backup frequency affects but repair time does not.

q: Which two outcomes depend directly on consistent resource tagging? (Choose two.)
opts: Encrypting the data stored on every resource that carries a tag
Automatically attributing cost to departments for showback or chargeback reports
Shortening restore time for resources after a failure occurs
Applying a shutdown schedule only to resources tagged as development
Blocking the accidental deletion of tagged resources
why: Tags are metadata that tools can filter and group on, which is what makes automatic cost attribution and policy targeting, such as shutting down only development resources, practical. A tag by itself does not encrypt data, speed up restores, or protect against deletion; those need separate controls, though a policy could be written to use tags as a selector.

q: An on-call team receives about 300 alerts a day, most informational and non-actionable, such as disk at 60%. Engineers have begun muting the channel, and a real outage alert was missed. What change most directly addresses the cause?
opts: Add more engineers to the on-call rotation to share the alert volume
Lower every threshold so that problems are caught even earlier
Page only urgent, actionable conditions; send the rest to tickets or dashboards
Replace paging entirely with a daily email digest of every alert
why: This is alert fatigue: so much low-value noise that people tune out the real signals. Reserving pages for urgent, actionable conditions and routing the rest elsewhere restores trust in the pager. Adding staff spreads the same noise across more people, lower thresholds produce even more alerts, and a daily digest would delay the notice of a real outage by hours.

q: During a change freeze, emergency changes can still be made, but they face added scrutiny and must be documented.
opts: True
False
why: A change freeze is a temporary, time-boxed tightening of change management, commonly around a seasonal peak or an audit. It does not make production untouchable: a genuine emergency still gets fixed, but with extra approval and a full record afterward.

q: An outage was caused by an engineer running a command against production instead of staging. Which two follow-up actions reflect a blameless review? (Choose two.)
opts: Issue a formal reprimand to the engineer who ran the command
Add a confirmation prompt and clear environment labeling to the tooling
Require the engineer to retrain and sign an acknowledgment of the incident
Skip root cause analysis since the cause was a single mistake
Document the timeline and contributing factors without assigning fault to an individual
why: A blameless review looks for the process and tooling gaps that made the mistake easy to make, and records the timeline honestly so people keep reporting what happened. Reprimands and mandatory sign-offs target the individual and discourage candor, and calling it a single mistake skips the root cause analysis that would find the missing safeguard.

q: An administrator has identified a connectivity problem and formed a theory that a specific firewall rule is blocking the traffic. Following the standard troubleshooting methodology, what should be done next?
opts: Document the incident as resolved, since the theory explains the symptoms
Test the theory by checking whether that rule actually denies the traffic
Verify full system functionality across all dependent services
Establish a plan of action, including rollback steps, to remove the rule
why: The methodology calls for testing the theory before acting on it, because a plausible theory that turns out to be wrong wastes a maintenance window or opens a security gap for nothing. Planning and implementing the fix comes after the theory is confirmed, verification comes after the fix, and documentation comes last.

q: A tenant's VM slows down at unpredictable times although its own workload and configuration are unchanged. Hypervisor metrics show another tenant on the same host consuming heavy CPU. Which action is most likely to resolve the problem from the affected tenant's side?
opts: Move the VM to a dedicated host or request migration to a different host
Reinstall the guest OS to clear accumulated resource usage
Add more vCPUs to the VM so it can claim a larger share
Increase the VM's disk size to improve I/O throughput
why: This is the noisy neighbor problem, caused by contention on shared hardware that the affected tenant cannot control from inside its own VM. The practical fixes are getting off that host or onto dedicated hardware, or having the provider apply resource governance. More vCPUs would only add to the contention, and reinstalling the OS or growing the disk does not touch the host-level cause.

q: A service is reachable by IP address from a virtual network but not by its hostname. A lookup against the network's default resolver returns NXDOMAIN, while a public resolver returns the correct address. What is the most likely cause?
opts: A firewall rule is blocking TCP traffic to the service's address
An MTU mismatch is silently dropping large packets along the path
The service's TLS certificate has expired and clients are rejecting it
The private DNS zone holding the record is missing or not linked to this network
why: Reaching the service by IP proves the network path and the service are healthy, and an NXDOMAIN from the network's own resolver while a public resolver answers points to a name resolution gap: the zone or record that resolver should consult is missing or not associated with this network. A firewall or MTU problem would also break access by IP, and an expired certificate would produce a TLS error rather than a failed lookup.

q: Upgrading a WAN link from 100 Mbps to 1 Gbps will fix slow interactive application responses that are caused by a 180 ms round-trip time.
opts: True
False
why: Bandwidth is how much data can move per unit of time once it is flowing, while latency is the delay before data starts to arrive. A round-trip time of 180 ms is mostly distance and path, so ten times the bandwidth leaves interactive responsiveness unchanged; fixes include moving the service closer to users or using a CDN or caching.

q: Restarting a hung service is a legitimate first response even when the cause is unknown, provided root cause analysis follows.
opts: True
False
why: A workaround that restores service quickly is reasonable under time pressure, and the mistake is stopping there. Root cause analysis afterward identifies why the service hung so the incident does not quietly repeat.

q: Which two steps belong between establishing a theory of probable cause and verifying full system functionality in the standard troubleshooting methodology? (Choose two.)
opts: Identify the problem by gathering information from users
Test the theory to confirm or rule out the probable cause
Document the findings, actions, and outcomes of the incident
Announce to users that the incident is closed for good
Establish a plan of action and implement the solution
why: The sequence is identify the problem, establish a theory, test the theory, establish a plan of action and implement the solution, verify full system functionality, and document. Testing the theory and planning and implementing the fix are the two steps in between. Identifying the problem comes before the theory, documentation comes after verification, and closing the incident is not a methodology step.

q: A service moved to a new IP address and its DNS record was updated. Some users still reach the old server while others reach the new one. Which two factors most plausibly explain this? (Choose two.)
opts: The new server's reverse (PTR) record was never created
Resolvers that cached the old record keep serving it until its TTL expires
The DNS zone has a syntax error that blocks all lookups for the domain
Some clients cached the old address locally or hard-coded it in a hosts file
The new server's TLS certificate expired before the cutover
why: Split behavior right after a DNS change is the signature of caching: resolvers that cached the old record serve it until the TTL expires, and some clients hold the old address locally or in a hosts file. A missing reverse record would not redirect anyone, a zone syntax error would fail lookups for everybody instead of sending some users to the old server, and an expired certificate would cause errors only for users who reach the new server.

q: Several VMs on the same virtualization host show consistently high "CPU ready" time in monitoring, even though each VM's own CPU utilization looks moderate. What does this metric specifically indicate?
opts: All the guest operating systems developed a memory leak at the same time
The host's physical CPUs are oversubscribed, so vCPUs wait in queue to be scheduled
The host's storage array is running short of IOPS, and the CPU metric is misleading
The VMs' NICs are on the wrong VLAN, and retransmissions look like CPU load
why: CPU ready time measures how long a vCPU is ready to run but must wait for a physical CPU to be scheduled. High values across several VMs on one host are the signature of CPU oversubscription and contention, even when each guest looks only moderately busy. A guest memory leak, a storage bottleneck, and a VLAN misconfiguration would not show up in this metric.

q: After a hypervisor host's clock drifts several minutes out of sync, users suddenly can't authenticate to a Kerberos-based service, and TLS certificate validation begins failing intermittently across VMs on that host, even though no configuration changed. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: Clock drift on the host because time synchronization (NTP) has stopped working
A DNS resolution failure between the VMs and the authentication server
A licensing limit reached on the authentication service host
Insufficient bandwidth between the VMs and the authentication server
why: Kerberos tickets and TLS certificates are both validated against the current time, so a clock that drifts by minutes makes valid tickets and certificates look expired or not yet valid. DNS, licensing, and bandwidth problems would not explain failures in two unrelated mechanisms that share only a dependency on accurate time.

q: New VMs being provisioned in a subnet intermittently fail to come online, with logs showing they never received an IP address. Existing VMs on the same subnet are unaffected. What is the most likely cause?
opts: The subnet's route table lacks a default route to the internet
The DNS records for the new VMs are missing from the zone
A load balancer health check is marking the new VMs unhealthy
The subnet's DHCP scope has no free addresses left to lease
why: New instances failing to get an address while running instances, which already hold leases, are unaffected is the classic sign of an exhausted DHCP scope. DNS records and health checks come into play only after a VM has an address, and a missing default route affects reaching the internet, not obtaining an IP address on the subnet.

q: In a two-node cluster, if the interconnect fails, quorum rules let either node safely continue as primary because each holds half of the votes.
opts: True
False
why: Quorum requires a majority of votes, and half is not a majority. With two nodes and no tie-breaker, neither side can prove it should be primary, so the cluster either stops or risks split-brain if both continue. That is why two-node clusters add a witness or third voting member.

q: A burstable VM becomes sluggish under sustained load. Which two observations would point to CPU credit exhaustion rather than a noisy neighbor? (Choose two.)
opts: CPU ready time is elevated on several unrelated VMs sharing the host
The instance's CPU credit balance has dropped to zero
Disk latency is also elevated for other tenants on the same storage
Throttling settles at a fixed baseline level regardless of other tenants' activity
The slowdown began at random times unrelated to this VM's own load
