why: A zero credit balance and a steady throttled baseline that does not depend on anyone else's activity are the fingerprints of credit exhaustion, which is an issue within the instance itself. Elevated CPU ready time on other VMs, shared storage latency, and slowdowns that strike at random times regardless of this VM's load all point to contention on the shared host instead.

q: A script launches 500 parallel calls to a provider's API and starts receiving HTTP 429 responses. The same calls succeed when the script sends about 10 per second. Which change best fixes the failures?
opts: Pace the requests and retry throttled calls with exponential backoff and jitter
Renew the API credentials, which have most likely expired
Retry every failed call immediately in a tight loop until it succeeds
Ask the provider to raise the account's service quota for this resource
why: HTTP 429 means the client is being rate limited, and the fact that the same calls succeed at a slower pace shows this is throttling, not a hard ceiling. Pacing the requests and backing off with jitter works with the limit. A quota increase is for a hard cap that fails at any speed, expired credentials would return an authentication error, and an immediate retry loop just keeps hitting the rate limit.

q: A database VM's queries have become noticeably slower. Which two metrics would most directly confirm that the storage subsystem is the bottleneck? (Choose two.)
opts: Network throughput on the VM's NIC approaching its limit
Disk queue length and I/O wait time consistently above baseline
Memory utilization steady at about 60% of the allocation
Read and write latency spiking well above its established baseline
High CPU utilization on the VM's vCPUs during the slowdown
why: Queue length, I/O wait, and read/write latency are direct measures of how the storage subsystem is performing, so elevated values against baseline confirm it as the bottleneck. NIC throughput, memory utilization, and CPU utilization measure other resources and would point toward network, memory, or compute bottlenecks if they were saturated.

q: Users report that one report in an application takes 40 seconds, while every other page, including login, is fast. A troubleshooter checks the browser's request timing, then the application server, then the database query, then the network. Which approach is this, and why does it suit the symptom?
opts: Bottom-up, because every layer must be checked starting from the cabling
Bottom-up, because network faults are the most common cause of slowness
Top-down, starting at the application layer because the symptom points there
Root cause analysis, because the problem is being fixed permanently
why: Starting at the layer closest to the user and working downward is the top-down approach, and it fits a symptom confined to one report, which points at the application or its query rather than at connectivity that every other page is using successfully. A bottom-up approach starts with the physical and network layers, which would waste time here, and root cause analysis is a goal rather than a layer-by-layer approach.

q: A VM shows normal CPU but heavy swap activity and intermittent slowness. The hypervisor dashboard shows its memory is being reclaimed through a balloon driver to serve other VMs on an overcommitted host. Which action most directly resolves the problem for this VM?
opts: Add more vCPUs so the VM can finish work faster
Enlarge the guest's swap file so paging has more room
Reserve the VM's memory so the hypervisor cannot reclaim it
Move the VM's disk to a faster storage tier
why: Ballooning takes memory from a VM and pushes the guest into swapping, so guaranteeing the VM's memory with a reservation stops the reclamation at its source. More vCPUs do not add memory, a bigger swap file only makes the slow paging more roomy, and faster storage reduces the penalty slightly without stopping the memory from being taken.

q: Two servers across a VPN tunnel can establish a connection and exchange small requests normally, but any transfer involving large packets consistently stalls or times out. What does this pattern most strongly suggest?
opts: Asymmetric routing causing replies to return over a different path
A missing authorization rule that rejects the clients' requests
The destination service has crashed and stopped accepting connections
An MTU mismatch causing oversized packets to be dropped instead of fragmented
why: Small packets succeeding while large ones consistently stall is the classic MTU mismatch signature: tunnel overhead shrinks the usable packet size, and oversized packets are dropped when fragmentation or path MTU discovery is not working. A crashed service or an authorization failure would break every request regardless of size, and asymmetric routing would not depend on packet size.

q: After a power event in one rack, several VMs on that rack's hosts lose all connectivity at the same time. Which troubleshooting approach reaches the cause most efficiently?
opts: Top-down, starting with each application's logs on every affected VM
Bottom-up, checking power, link status, and the physical network first
Restarting every affected VM and observing which ones recover
Top-down, starting with the database queries behind each application
why: Simultaneous total connectivity loss for everything in a rack right after a power event points to the physical and network layers, so a bottom-up approach that checks power, links, and switches first gets to the cause fastest. Top-down approaches start at the application, where nothing is wrong, and restarting VMs treats symptoms without testing any theory.

q: A three-node cluster loses connectivity between node C and nodes A and B, which can still talk to each other. Which two outcomes are consistent with quorum and fencing working correctly? (Choose two.)
opts: Node C keeps accepting writes because it still believes it is primary
Nodes A and B hold a majority and continue operating as the primary side
Nodes A and B stop because the cluster no longer has all three members
Node C, lacking quorum, stops serving writes and may be fenced off
All three nodes accept writes until the partition heals, then merge
why: Quorum lets the two-node majority keep running, while the isolated node that lost quorum must stop accepting writes, and fencing can forcibly isolate or power it off to be sure. Letting node C or all three nodes keep writing is exactly the split-brain that these mechanisms prevent, and quorum needs only a majority, not every member, so A and B do not need to stop.

q: A burstable-type VM instance was fast immediately after being resized, but a few hours into a sustained CPU-heavy job it drops to a much lower, steady level of performance, even though CPU utilization in monitoring still shows high demand. What does this pattern most strongly suggest?
opts: The instance's CPU credit balance ran out, throttling it to baseline performance
Another tenant on the same host started a heavy workload around the same time
A software license core limit was reached on the instance
A stale cached DNS answer is sending the traffic to a distant server
why: Burstable instances spend CPU credits during high demand and are throttled to a fixed baseline when the balance hits zero, which produces fast performance at first and a lower steady rate after a few hours of sustained load. A noisy neighbor would not depend on how long this instance has been busy and would not settle at a steady level, and licensing and DNS do not cause a gradual, time-dependent performance drop.

q: A cached result used by thousands of clients expires at the same moment, and all of them immediately request it from the origin, briefly overwhelming it even though the origin handles the same volume easily when spread out. Which change best prevents a repeat?
opts: Scale the origin vertically to the largest instance size available
Shorten the cache TTL so that entries are refreshed more often
Switch the load balancer from round robin to least connections
Add random jitter to cache expiry times so entries do not all expire together
why: This is a thundering herd: a synchronized event makes everyone act at once. Randomizing expiry times spreads the refreshes over time, which is the standard fix. Scaling the origin chases a peak that exists only because requests are synchronized, a shorter TTL creates more synchronized expirations, and changing the balancing algorithm does not reduce the size of the simultaneous surge.

q: After a second network path is added for redundancy, a connection establishes but then intermittently stalls. A stateful firewall's log shows packets arriving that match no connection it tracked as outbound. What is the most likely cause?
opts: An MTU mismatch on the new path, dropping any packet above a certain size
Asymmetric routing: replies return over a path that did not carry the request
The firewall's connection table is full and dropping new sessions
The destination's API is throttling this client with 429 responses
why: A stateful firewall recognizes return traffic only for connections it saw leave. If replies come back over the new path while requests leave over the old one, the firewall has no record of them and may drop them, which is asymmetric routing introduced by the redundant path. A full connection table would reject new sessions rather than orphan replies, an MTU problem depends on packet size, and API throttling would not show as untracked packets at the firewall.

q: A container is observed repeatedly starting, failing within a few seconds, and being automatically restarted by the orchestrator, over and over. Monitoring shows this as a series of short up-and-down cycles rather than one continuous outage. Where should an engineer look first to find the actual cause?
opts: The load balancer's health check thresholds and interval
Memory ballooning statistics on the underlying hypervisor host
The container's own startup logs from one of its failed attempts
The DNS TTL configured on the service's public record
why: A crash loop is caused by something failing inside the container on every start, such as a bad configuration, a missing dependency, or an application error, so the container's own startup logs from a failed attempt show the cause. Health check settings, host memory ballooning, and DNS TTL are not why a container fails on each of its own startup attempts.

q: An automation script calling a cloud provider's API begins failing every single call to create a new VM in a particular region, always with the same error citing a maximum resource count for that region, regardless of how much the script slows down between calls. What kind of limit is this?
opts: A service quota, resolved by requesting an increase rather than retrying slowly
A licensing capacity limit on the operating system being deployed
API throttling, which would clear if the script simply retried more slowly
An expired TLS certificate on the endpoint the script calls
why: Failing every attempt at any pace against a fixed resource count is a hard service quota, and the fix is to request an increase. Throttling is pace-dependent and would clear with slower calls, and neither OS licensing nor an expired certificate would produce an error that cites a regional resource maximum.

q: VM A slows at random times regardless of its own load and recovers within minutes with no action. VM B always slows after two to three hours of sustained load and takes hours of light use to recover. Which two diagnoses fit these patterns? (Choose two.)
opts: VM A: exhausted CPU credits on a burstable instance
VM A: contention from another tenant on its host
VM B: contention from another tenant on its host
Both VMs: a stale cached DNS answer returned by a resolver
VM B: exhausted CPU credits that rebuild slowly during light use
why: Random slowdowns unrelated to the VM's own load that clear by themselves fit contention from another tenant, which comes and goes with the neighbor's activity. A slowdown that appears after sustained load and recovers only slowly fits a burstable instance's credits, which are spent under load and rebuilt gradually. Swapping the diagnoses reverses the timing behaviors, and a stale DNS answer would not degrade performance in either pattern.

q: If traceroute shows 100% loss at hop 5 but hops 6 through 10 respond normally, hop 5 is where traffic is being dropped.
opts: True
False
why: Routers often deprioritize or rate-limit the ICMP replies they generate for themselves, so a single hop can show loss without dropping forwarded traffic. If later hops respond normally, packets are clearly passing through hop 5, so the real problem is elsewhere or the hop is simply not answering probes.

q: Autoscaling flapping is fixed the same way an overly sensitive alert is: widen the gap between the scale-out and scale-in triggers or add a cooldown period, rather than raising the maximum instance count.
opts: True
False
why: Flapping happens when scale-out and scale-in thresholds sit too close to ordinary load variation, so normal fluctuation keeps crossing them in both directions. A wider margin or a cooldown stops the oscillation, whereas a higher maximum instance count only changes how far scaling can go.

q: Users report intermittent packet loss to a service, and ping from a client confirms about 10% loss. Which two next steps are most appropriate? (Choose two.)
opts: Restart the service, since hung connections usually cause packet loss
Run traceroute or a path-monitoring tool to find the hop where loss begins
Order a higher-bandwidth circuit, since loss means the link is full
Capture packets on both ends to see whether lost packets leave and arrive
Reinstall the client's network drivers and operating system
why: Ping has confirmed the problem, so the next steps narrow down where it occurs: a hop-by-hop trace shows where along the path loss begins, and captures at both ends show whether packets are lost in transit. Restarting the service, buying bandwidth, or reinstalling client software are guesses that skip diagnosis, and none of them is supported by the evidence so far.

q: Which two practices make timestamp-based correlation of logs from many systems reliable? (Choose two.)
opts: Encrypting each log file at rest on the system that produced it
Keeping all systems' clocks synchronized with a common time source such as NTP
Compressing logs before they are forwarded to the central platform
Writing timestamps in one consistent format and time zone, such as UTC
Rotating logs daily so that each file stays small and quick to open
why: Lining up events by time only works if every system's clock agrees and every log expresses time the same way, so synchronized clocks and a consistent format and time zone are what make the timeline trustworthy. Encryption, compression, and rotation have their own purposes but do not affect whether timestamps from different systems can be compared.
